title: Molecular Genetics

lessons.title: Evidence that DNA carries genetic information
lessons.question: What made DNA a stronger explanation of heredity than protein?
lessons.goal: Connect each experiment with its observation, control and justified conclusion.
lessons.prior: Genes are inherited units. Identifying the molecule that carries them requires evidence, not just finding a molecule inside a cell.

terms.meaning: A heritable change associated with a cell taking up external genetic material.
terms.example: A bacterial lineage acquires a trait after exposure to material from other cells.
terms.importantDistinction: Griffith demonstrated transformation without identifying DNA as the active substance.
terms.misconception: Griffith’s result alone identified the molecular structure of DNA.

terms.meaning: Material that stores and transmits inherited biological information.
terms.example: DNA carries genetic information in the cellular systems studied here.
terms.importantDistinction: A molecule’s presence in a cell is not sufficient evidence that it carries heredity.
terms.misconception: Any abundant cellular molecule must be the hereditary material.

terms.meaning: A detectable radioactive label used to follow the movement of material.
terms.example: Different labels followed phage DNA and protein in separate preparations.
terms.importantDistinction: A tracer follows the labelled material, not every molecule in the mixture.
terms.misconception: A tracer automatically proves the function of every labelled molecule.

terms.meaning: A comparison designed to distinguish explanations by changing a relevant factor while keeping others comparable.
terms.example: DNA-destroying treatment is compared with other treatments of a transforming preparation.
terms.importantDistinction: The interpretation depends on what was changed and what was measured.
terms.misconception: A single observation without comparison always proves a mechanism.

sections: Griffith established a transferable change

Griffith studied bacteria with different disease-causing properties. Live non-virulent bacteria could acquire a heritable virulent trait when mixed with heat-killed virulent bacteria. Material from the killed cells had changed the living bacterial lineage.
This result supported transformation. It did not identify the transforming substance. DNA and protein were among the candidates, so the next question was which component was necessary for the change.
Remove a candidate and test the effect

Avery, MacLeod and McCarty studied transforming preparations and used treatments aimed at different components. When DNA was destroyed, transforming activity was lost. Comparable treatments directed at other components did not remove activity in the same way.

This was stronger evidence for DNA because the experiment connected an intervention with the loss of a measured function. The useful comparison is not simply that DNA was present. It is that destroying DNA disrupted transformation under the experimental conditions.
Trace the material entering infected cells

Hershey and Chase used bacteriophages, viruses that infect bacteria. In separate preparations, phosphorus-32 labelled viral DNA and sulfur-35 labelled viral protein. After infection, they separated much of the external phage material from the bacterial cells.

The DNA label was associated much more strongly with the infected cells than the external protein label. This supported DNA as the material entering the cells and directing viral production in that system.

Together the experiments built a case for DNA as hereditary material. They did not by themselves explain its double-helical structure or every step of gene expression. Match each scientist with the specific question their evidence addressed.

lessons.title: DNA structure and complementary strands
lessons.question: How does DNA’s structure provide a way to copy information?
lessons.goal: Identify nucleotide components, complementary base pairing and antiparallel strand directions.
lessons.prior: DNA carries inherited information. A structure that can be copied must provide a rule for constructing a matching strand.

terms.meaning: A nucleic-acid subunit containing a sugar, phosphate and nitrogenous base.
terms.example: A DNA nucleotide contains deoxyribose, phosphate and one of A, T, C or G.
terms.importantDistinction: A base is one component of a nucleotide, not the whole nucleotide.
terms.misconception: A nucleotide consists of three amino acids.

terms.meaning: Specific pairing of bases across nucleic-acid strands.
terms.example: In double-stranded DNA, A pairs with T and C with G.
terms.importantDistinction: The paired strands are complementary, not identical sequences in the same direction.
terms.misconception: A pairs with C in the standard DNA model.

terms.meaning: Oriented in opposite directions.
terms.example: One aligned DNA strand runs 5′ to 3′ while its partner runs 3′ to 5′.
terms.importantDistinction: Read the direction labels before copying a displayed sequence.
terms.misconception: Both aligned DNA strands run 5′ to 3′ from left to right.

terms.meaning: The equality of A with T and C with G in standard double-stranded DNA.
terms.example: If A is 30% of a double-stranded sample, T is also 30%.
terms.importantDistinction: A plus T need not equal C plus G.
terms.misconception: Every DNA sample must have 25% of each base.

sections: Build a nucleotide before building a helix

DNA is a polymer: a long chain made from nucleotide subunits. Each DNA nucleotide contains deoxyribose sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base. The four bases are adenine, thymine, cytosine and guanine, abbreviated A, T, C and G.

Sugars and phosphates form the backbone of each strand. Bases project inward and pair with bases on the other strand. Covalent bonds hold the backbone together; hydrogen bonds connect complementary bases across the strands. These are different connections and perform different structural roles.
Pairing and direction are separate rules

In the standard double-stranded DNA model, A pairs with T and C pairs with G. A and G are double-ring purines; C and T are single-ring pyrimidines. A purine paired with a pyrimidine helps maintain a consistent width.

The strands are antiparallel. If an upper strand is written 5′-ATGC-3′, its aligned partner is 3′-TACG-5′. If you must report that partner in the 5′ to 3′ direction, reverse the displayed order: 5′-GCAT-3′.

The numbers identify positions in the sugar and therefore strand orientation. They do not identify the first and third bases in a codon. Direction becomes essential when interpreting replication and transcription.
Use proportions without assuming equal amounts

Chargaff’s observations supported equality between A and T, and between C and G, in double-stranded DNA. If A accounts for 30% of all bases, T is 30%, leaving 40% for C and G together. Each is therefore 20%.

Franklin’s X-ray diffraction work provided important structural evidence. Watson and Crick developed a double-helix model consistent with that evidence and the base relationships. Structure, chemical composition and inherited function were connected by different lines of investigation.
Do not apply equal A/T proportions to every single strand by itself. The equalities arise from the complementary double-stranded molecule.

lessons.title: DNA replication and its products
lessons.question: Why can only one side of a replication fork be copied continuously?
lessons.goal: Trace semiconservative replication using base pairing, enzyme roles and the 5′ to 3′ synthesis rule.
lessons.prior: DNA strands are complementary and antiparallel. During S phase, DNA amount increases before cell division.

terms.meaning: Replication producing DNA molecules with one parental strand and one newly synthesized strand.
terms.example: After one replication, both daughter molecules contain an old strand paired with a new strand.
terms.importantDistinction: The original strands are retained in separate daughter molecules.
terms.misconception: Semiconservative replication leaves both old strands together in one daughter molecule.

terms.meaning: An enzyme that extends a new DNA strand by adding nucleotides to its 3′ end.
terms.example: Complementary nucleotides extend a primed strand in the 5′ to 3′ direction.
terms.importantDistinction: It synthesizes 5′ to 3′ while reading an antiparallel template.
terms.misconception: DNA polymerase extends a new strand equally well in either direction.

terms.meaning: A short newly synthesized DNA segment on the lagging strand.
terms.example: Several fragments are made as new lagging-strand template becomes exposed.
terms.importantDistinction: Each fragment is still synthesized 5′ to 3′.
terms.misconception: Lagging-strand fragments are synthesized 3′ to 5′.

terms.meaning: An enzyme that seals breaks in the sugar-phosphate backbone.
terms.example: It joins adjacent DNA segments after primer replacement.
terms.importantDistinction: Ligase seals backbone connections; helicase separates paired strands.
terms.misconception: Ligase opens the DNA double helix by breaking base-pair hydrogen bonds.

sections: Use each parental strand as a template

Replication begins at an origin and opens a region of the DNA. Helicase separates the paired strands by disrupting their hydrogen-bond interactions. It does not cut each strand’s sugar-phosphate backbone into small pieces.
Each parental strand provides a template for a complementary new strand. The two resulting DNA molecules each contain one old strand and one new strand. This is semiconservative replication.

Meselson and Stahl followed DNA density after cells moved from a heavy-nitrogen medium to a light-nitrogen medium. The first generation produced intermediate-density DNA. In the second, intermediate and light DNA appeared. This pattern supported semiconservative replication over the alternatives tested.
A primer provides a starting point
DNA polymerase cannot begin a new strand from nothing. Primase makes a short RNA primer that supplies a starting 3′ end. DNA polymerase then extends from that end with complementary DNA nucleotides.
New DNA is always synthesized 5′ to 3′. Because the parental templates run in opposite directions, their new strands cannot both follow the moving replication fork continuously.

The leading strand is synthesized continuously toward the fork. The lagging strand is made in Okazaki fragments, each extending 5′ to 3′ away from the fork as additional template is exposed. Each fragment requires a primer.
Finish the backbone and check the result

RNA primers are removed and replaced with DNA through the replication machinery. DNA ligase seals the remaining backbone breaks between adjacent segments. Proofreading and repair reduce errors, although some DNA changes can persist.
Use the enzyme names to explain different jobs: helicase opens, primase starts, DNA polymerase extends, and ligase joins. Do not use the word “copies” as if one enzyme performs every part.
Replication increases DNA amount but does not by itself separate sister chromatids into daughter cells. Cell division is a later process.

lessons.title: Genes, RNA and the flow of information
lessons.question: How can cells with similar DNA perform different jobs?
lessons.goal: Distinguish DNA storage from RNA and protein roles, and explain selective gene expression.
lessons.prior: A DNA sequence contains information. Different cells need different combinations and amounts of functional products.

terms.meaning: The use of genetic information to produce a functional RNA or protein product.
terms.example: A cell produces a particular protein by transcribing and translating the relevant gene.
terms.importantDistinction: Not every gene is expressed equally in every cell.
terms.misconception: Every cell continuously makes every possible protein.

terms.meaning: RNA that carries a sequence used to direct protein synthesis.
terms.example: A processed mRNA moves from the nucleus to a ribosome.
terms.importantDistinction: It carries a working copy; the DNA molecule need not leave the nucleus.
terms.misconception: Messenger RNA is a chain of amino acids.

terms.meaning: RNA that helps match an mRNA codon with its corresponding amino acid.
terms.example: A charged tRNA pairs its anticodon with a codon at the ribosome.
terms.importantDistinction: The amino acid is attached to tRNA, not directly specified by a DNA molecule at the ribosome.
terms.misconception: Transfer RNA carries a complete chromosome.

terms.meaning: RNA that forms structural and catalytic parts of ribosomes.
terms.example: Ribosomal RNA contributes to the machinery that links amino acids.
terms.importantDistinction: Ribosomes also contain proteins.
terms.misconception: A ribosome is made only of DNA.

sections: A shared genome does not require identical activity

Many nucleated somatic cells contain essentially the same inherited genome, yet muscle, nerve and other cells perform different tasks. They express different sets of genes and produce different amounts of particular products.

Gene expression is not the same as changing the DNA sequence. A cell can change which genes are active without replacing every gene it contains. Some genes produce functional RNA rather than a protein.
Separate the molecules and their jobs

DNA generally stores information in a double-stranded molecule using deoxyribose and the bases A, T, C and G. RNA uses ribose and uracil, U, instead of thymine. RNA is usually single-stranded but can fold through base pairing within the molecule.

For a protein-coding gene, transcription produces RNA from a DNA template. Translation uses the mRNA sequence to assemble amino acids into a polypeptide. The commonly taught information pathway is DNA → RNA → protein.

Messenger RNA carries the sequence, transfer RNA brings matched amino acids, and ribosomal RNA forms part of the ribosome’s structure and catalytic machinery. These RNA types have different roles even though all are nucleic acids.
Locate the processes in a eukaryotic cell

For the nuclear genes considered here, transcription occurs in the nucleus. The RNA is processed, and mature mRNA can leave through nuclear pores. Translation occurs at ribosomes in the cytoplasm, including ribosomes associated with rough endoplasmic reticulum.
A protein’s amino-acid sequence influences how it folds and functions. A different sequence may change that function, but not every sequence difference has an equally large effect.

Do not describe non-protein-coding DNA as automatically useless. Some sequences regulate expression, and some genes produce functional RNAs. This chapter focuses on protein synthesis without claiming that it explains every DNA function.

lessons.title: Transcription and RNA processing
lessons.question: Which DNA strand is used to make the RNA message?
lessons.goal: Use template and coding strand identities to construct mRNA and explain eukaryotic RNA processing.
lessons.prior: Complementary strands are antiparallel. RNA uses U where DNA uses T.

terms.meaning: The DNA strand read by RNA polymerase to construct complementary RNA.
terms.example: A 3′-TAC-5′ template segment produces 5′-AUG-3′ RNA.
terms.importantDistinction: It is complementary to the RNA, rather than matching its sequence.
terms.misconception: The template strand always has the same sequence as mRNA.

terms.meaning: The DNA strand whose 5′ to 3′ sequence matches the RNA sequence apart from T versus U.
terms.example: Coding DNA 5′-ATG-3′ corresponds to mRNA 5′-AUG-3′.
terms.importantDistinction: It is not the strand read as the template for that transcript.
terms.misconception: RNA polymerase must copy the coding strand as its complementary template.

terms.meaning: An enzyme that synthesizes RNA using a DNA template.
terms.example: It reads the template 3′ to 5′ while extending RNA 5′ to 3′.
terms.importantDistinction: Transcription uses RNA nucleotides and does not require Okazaki fragments.
terms.misconception: RNA polymerase builds a polypeptide from amino acids.

terms.meaning: Removal of introns and joining of retained exon sequences in a pre-mRNA.
terms.example: A eukaryotic precursor is processed before mature mRNA is exported.
terms.importantDistinction: Retained exon sequence can include untranslated regions as well as coding regions.
terms.misconception: Every sequence retained in an exon must be translated into an amino acid.

sections: Read the template, not the label you remember

RNA polymerase binds at a gene’s regulatory starting region and opens a short DNA region. It reads the template strand in the 3′ to 5′ direction while building complementary RNA 5′ to 3′. Only one DNA strand serves as the template for a particular transcript.

A on the DNA template pairs with U in RNA; T pairs with A; C pairs with G; G pairs with C. The other DNA strand is called the coding strand because its 5′ to 3′ sequence matches the RNA sequence except that DNA has T and RNA has U.

For example, template 3′-TAC GGA-5′ produces mRNA 5′-AUG CCU-3′. Its coding DNA partner is 5′-ATG CCT-3′. Identify which strand you have before deciding whether to complement or simply replace T with U.
An RNA message is not a new DNA helix

Transcription copies the information of a selected DNA region into RNA. The DNA strands close behind the enzyme and the RNA separates. It does not copy the entire genome in the same way as S-phase replication.

Because one continuous RNA molecule is synthesized from one template, transcription does not require a leading strand, lagging strand or Okazaki fragments. Those terms belong to DNA replication at a fork.
Process the eukaryotic transcript
A newly made eukaryotic pre-mRNA is commonly processed before export. Introns are removed, and exons are joined. A cap and a poly-A tail help protect the message and support its use by the cell.
Introns are removed from the RNA, not normally cut out of the genomic DNA during this processing step. Exons are the portions retained in the mature RNA; some retained sequence is not translated.

Once processing is complete, the mature message can leave the nucleus. Keep transcription, RNA processing and translation as distinct steps even though they contribute to one overall gene-expression pathway.

lessons.title: Translation and the genetic code
lessons.question: How do nucleotide triplets become an amino-acid sequence?
lessons.goal: Use mRNA codons, tRNA anticodons and start/stop signals to explain polypeptide synthesis.
lessons.prior: A mature mRNA is read 5′ to 3′. Its sequence differs from a DNA template and uses uracil.

terms.meaning: A three-nucleotide sequence in mRNA interpreted during translation.
terms.example: AUG specifies methionine and commonly serves as a start codon.
terms.importantDistinction: Use mRNA 5′ to 3′ to consult a codon table.
terms.misconception: A codon is a triplet of amino acids.

terms.meaning: A tRNA triplet that pairs antiparallel with an mRNA codon.
terms.example: 3′-UAC-5′ pairs with mRNA 5′-AUG-3′.
terms.importantDistinction: A codon table is organized by mRNA codons, not by anticodons.
terms.misconception: The anticodon is identical to its paired mRNA codon.

terms.meaning: The grouping of a nucleotide sequence into successive triplets for translation.
terms.example: Beginning at a different position changes which bases form each codon.
terms.importantDistinction: The position of the start establishes which triplets are read.

sections: Read the message in triplets

A ribosome reads mRNA in successive three-nucleotide codons. Each amino-acid codon specifies one amino acid in the standard code. Several different codons can specify the same amino acid; this redundancy does not mean one codon specifies several amino acids at once.

AUG commonly acts as a start codon and specifies methionine. Starting at the correct AUG establishes the reading frame. A sequence written for codon practice may instead be identified as an internal coding segment; follow that instruction rather than assuming every short fragment contains the beginning of a full gene.
Match and join
A tRNA carries an amino acid and has an anticodon that can pair with a complementary mRNA codon. The strands pair antiparallel. For mRNA 5′-AUG-3′, an aligned anticodon is 3′-UAC-5′.

Ribosomes contain rRNA and proteins. As matching tRNAs enter and the ribosome moves along the mRNA, amino acids are linked by peptide bonds. The growing chain is a polypeptide, which can later fold and undergo additional processing.
The mRNA is not physically converted into protein. It is read as information while amino acids are assembled from a separate supply.
Stop at the signal and use the right table
UAA, UAG and UGA are stop codons in the standard code. A release factor helps terminate translation and release the chain. A stop codon does not recruit a tRNA carrying a “stop amino acid.”

Always use the mRNA codon, written 5′ to 3′, when looking up an amino acid. Convert a DNA template or anticodon first. A protein chain is described by amino-acid order; it does not have DNA-style 5′ and 3′ ends.
Use the codon reference included in this course. It provides the information needed for sequence questions without requiring a separate data booklet.

sections: Write the problem’s identity line first

Before changing any letters, write four things: the supplied molecule, its strand identity if it is DNA, the displayed direction, and the requested output. “DNA” alone is insufficient when a question expects an unambiguous mRNA sequence.

For coding DNA written 5′ to 3′, replace T with U. For template DNA written 3′ to 5′, construct the complementary RNA from left to right. For template DNA written 5′ to 3′, the RNA must be constructed from the template’s opposite end and reported 5′ to 3′.
Keep the direction labels visible until the final check. Removing them early is a common reason for getting correct pairings in the wrong order.
Establish the frame before translating

For a complete simplified message, begin at the specified start AUG and stop at the first in-frame stop codon. Divide the sequence into triplets only after establishing the start. Bases before the start are not automatically translated.

For an explicitly stated internal coding segment, use the supplied reading frame. Such an exercise can ask for amino-acid identities without including the beginning of the protein. Do not invent a start or stop that the question does not provide.

A stretch coding for five amino acids contains fifteen coding nucleotides. An additional stop codon requires three more nucleotides but does not add an amino acid. State whether the question includes that signal.
Check the result in both directions
Compare each RNA base with the template and compare the RNA with the coding DNA partner. Then consult the codon table one triplet at a time. Check that a stop has not been counted as an amino acid.
Several RNA sequences can produce the same peptide because of code redundancy. From a protein sequence alone, you can often give a possible RNA sequence, but not a unique original sequence.
The short sequences in these exercises are constructed teaching examples, not complete human genes or laboratory protocols.

lessons.title: Mutations and their effects on proteins
lessons.question: Why can a one-base change have no effect, a small effect or a major effect?
lessons.goal: Distinguish a DNA mutation from expression errors and explain substitution, frameshift and inheritance consequences.
lessons.prior: Protein sequence depends on the mRNA reading frame and the genetic code. Several codons can specify the same amino acid.

terms.meaning: A persistent change in a DNA sequence.
terms.example: A DNA base substitution remains after replication and repair.
terms.importantDistinction: An error in one RNA or protein molecule is not automatically a DNA mutation.

terms.meaning: A shift in reading frame caused by an insertion or deletion not divisible by three in a coding region.

sections: Locate the change in DNA

A mutation is a persistent DNA sequence change. It may arise from replication errors or DNA damage that is not accurately repaired. An error during transcription or translation can alter an individual product without changing the DNA template itself.

A substitution replaces one base with another. In a coding region, its consequence depends on the resulting mRNA codon. A silent substitution leaves the amino acid unchanged; a missense substitution changes an amino acid; a nonsense mutation introduces a premature stop.
Check the code rather than guessing severity

Consider the internal mRNA coding segment CAG UUA CCC. It specifies Gln–Leu–Pro. Changing UUA to UUG still gives leucine, a silent substitution. Changing UUA to UCA gives serine, a missense change. Changing it to UAA creates a stop signal.

The size of a change in DNA does not by itself determine the effect on the organism. Protein location, function, remaining sequence and other biological factors matter. A missense change can be important or relatively minor; a premature stop can remove a critical region.
Track the frame and the lineage

An insertion or deletion of one nucleotide shifts the downstream triplet grouping. Insertions or deletions not divisible by three can therefore cause a frameshift in a translated region. Removing exactly three bases may remove an amino acid without shifting later codons.

A somatic mutation occurs in a body-cell lineage. It can affect that organism and descendant cells without usually entering its gametes. A germ-line mutation can be transmitted if it is present in a gamete that contributes to an offspring. “Can be inherited” does not mean every offspring receives it.
Mutations create new sequence variants. Selection and other population processes determine how their frequencies change; organisms do not produce the exact mutation they need on demand.

lessons.title: Recombination and sources of variation
lessons.question: How can new allele combinations arise without a new mutation at every gene?
lessons.goal: Distinguish mutation, recombination and transfer of existing genetic material.
lessons.prior: Mutations change sequences. Meiosis can rearrange existing alleles among chromosomes and gametes.

terms.meaning: The production of new combinations of genetic material.
terms.example: Crossing over creates chromosomes carrying new combinations of existing alleles.
terms.importantDistinction: A new combination does not require every allele to be newly mutated.

sections: Separate new sequences from new combinations

A mutation can create a new allele. Recombination can bring existing alleles together in new arrangements. During meiosis, crossing over exchanges corresponding DNA between non-sister chromatids, and independent assortment distributes homologues into gametes.

Random fertilization adds another level of combination. An offspring can therefore differ from both parents without every difference requiring a new mutation. Keep the origin of a sequence variant separate from its reassortment.
Bacteria exchange genetic material in several ways

Bacteria normally reproduce by binary fission, but they can also acquire DNA from other sources. Transformation involves uptake of external DNA. Conjugation involves direct contact and transfer, often including plasmids. Transduction involves a virus carrying bacterial genetic material.

These mechanisms can introduce traits into a bacterial lineage. They are not the same as mitosis or the production and fusion of animal gametes. The important question is how the DNA enters and how it can persist in descendants.
A transferred sequence must be maintained and expressed in an appropriate context to affect a phenotype. Detecting DNA outside a cell is not enough to establish a stable inherited change.
Mitochondrial DNA records a particular lineage

Mitochondria contain their own DNA, consistent with their evolutionary origin through endosymbiosis. In the usual human model, mitochondrial inheritance is predominantly maternal because the egg contributes the mitochondria retained in the embryo.

Comparing mtDNA can inform relationships along maternal lineages. It does not represent the entire nuclear genome or all branches of ancestry. Similarity of a short sequence is evidence to interpret, not a complete family history.
Do not assume mitochondrial variants are always harmless. Like other sequence changes, their effects depend on the genes and biological processes involved.

lessons.title: Recombinant DNA and genetic engineering
lessons.question: What must happen for a transferred gene to produce a useful product?
lessons.goal: Explain the conceptual roles of restriction enzymes, ligase, vectors and expression in recombinant-DNA technology.
lessons.prior: Genes carry sequences, but a cell must have a compatible expression system to use them.

terms.meaning: A DNA molecule assembled from genetic material from different sources.
terms.example: A plasmid carries an inserted coding sequence.
terms.importantDistinction: Recombinant DNA describes the assembled molecule, not a guarantee of protein production.
terms.misconception: Any mixture of separate DNA molecules is automatically a functional recombinant gene.

terms.meaning: An enzyme that cuts DNA at particular recognition sequences.
terms.example: Matching cuts can create compatible ends on an insert and vector.

terms.misconception: Restriction enzymes cut every DNA molecule at an arbitrary identical distance.

terms.meaning: A small DNA molecule used to carry an inserted sequence into a host.
terms.example: An engineered bacterial plasmid carries a coding sequence and appropriate regulatory elements.
terms.importantDistinction: A plasmid is not the whole bacterial chromosome.
terms.misconception: A plasmid is a membrane-bounded nucleus.

terms.meaning: The regulatory and cellular context that allows a gene’s product to be made.
terms.example: A host requires suitable signals to transcribe and translate an inserted sequence.
terms.importantDistinction: An inserted DNA sequence is not automatically expressed in every host.

sections: Join a sequence with a carrier

Genetic engineering can assemble DNA from different sources. A vector carries a sequence into a host where it may be maintained and expressed. Plasmids are one type of vector; they are small DNA molecules separate from the main bacterial chromosome.

Restriction enzymes recognize particular DNA sequences and cut the backbone. Some cuts leave overhanging “sticky ends” that can pair with complementary ends. DNA ligase seals the backbone connections to form a joined molecule.
Matching ends help the pieces fit, but simply mixing DNA is not enough to guarantee the correct arrangement or a functional product.
Make the information usable by the host

A transferred gene must be linked to appropriate expression signals and interpreted by the host machinery. Many human genes contain introns. Bacteria do not normally process human introns in the same way as human cells, so a suitable intron-free coding sequence may be used.

Complementary DNA, or cDNA, can be made from a processed RNA template. This provides one route to an intron-free sequence. The conceptual point is that the host must receive usable coding information, not just any piece cut from a human chromosome.

Production of a human protein in bacteria therefore depends on both the sequence and the expression context. The insulin example illustrates a biological manufacturing principle rather than a complete laboratory protocol.
Verify several different claims

Finding an insert shows that DNA is present. Detecting its RNA supports transcription. Detecting the intended protein supports expression, while demonstrating its biological activity tests function. These are related but distinct claims.

A useful evaluation asks what was changed, what product was measured, how it was compared with a control and whether unintended effects were examined. Avoid treating “genetically modified” as a single guaranteed outcome shared by all organisms and technologies.
Use the mechanism to interpret evidence. Do not infer safety, effectiveness or environmental performance solely from a technology’s name.

lessons.question: What can a banding pattern support, and what can it not prove?
lessons.goal: Explain DNA amplification and fragment separation, then interpret profiles within their limits.

terms.example: A defined region is copied many times using primers and a heat-stable polymerase.

sections: Amplify a selected region

PCR increases the amount of a selected DNA region. Repeated cycles separate the strands, allow primers to bind, and use a heat-stable DNA polymerase to extend new strands. Primers define the region to be copied.

In an idealized model, each complete cycle doubles the number of target molecules. Starting from one target molecule, three ideal cycles produce eight. Real reactions may not double perfectly throughout, so the model is a calculation aid rather than a guarantee about every experiment.
Read a gel from wells toward the positive end

DNA has a negative charge because of its phosphate backbone. In a standard DNA gel, an electric field draws fragments toward the positive electrode. Smaller fragments usually travel farther through the gel than larger fragments under the same conditions.
Samples are loaded into separate lanes. A DNA ladder provides fragments of known sizes for comparison. Identify the wells, migration direction and ladder before interpreting a band position.
A band represents many molecules of similar length, not one whole cell. Two fragments can have the same length without necessarily having identical sequences.
Compare patterns without overstating identity

DNA profiling compares selected markers rather than reading every nucleotide in the genome. In a simplified classroom matching problem, compare the complete supplied pattern, not just one shared band. Excluding a sample that lacks required bands differs from proving every circumstance associated with a compatible sample.

In a simplified parentage exercise, each child marker must be explainable by inheritance from the proposed parents. Account for the maternal contributions before comparing the remaining markers with possible paternal contributions.

Actual interpretation also considers laboratory quality, contamination, relatedness and statistical evidence. A classroom gel cannot by itself establish guilt, consent or the circumstances in which material was deposited.

lessons.question: How do we distinguish a promising result from an unsupported claim?

sections: Identify what the technology actually does

Sequencing determines base order. PCR increases copies of a selected region. Recombinant-DNA methods assemble genetic material, while cloning may refer to copies of DNA, cells or whole organisms. These terms are related but not interchangeable.

A proposed gene-based intervention might replace missing function, alter expression or change a sequence in target cells. Its success depends on reaching the appropriate cells, achieving the intended change and avoiding unacceptable unintended effects.
A result in one cell type or experimental system cannot automatically be generalized to every tissue or organism.
Separate a measured result from a broad claim

Suppose a hypothetical intervention increases production of a protein in cultured cells. That supports a change in expression under those conditions. It does not alone demonstrate improved organ function, long-term benefit or acceptable safety in a whole organism.

A stronger evaluation would ask about comparison groups, reproducibility, functional measurements, unintended changes and duration. These are questions about the evidence needed, not a prediction that every promising technology will succeed or fail.
The examples here teach how to evaluate mechanisms and claims. They are not recommendations for personal testing, treatment or laboratory work.
Include people and environments in the question

Genetic information can affect individuals and biological relatives. Research and applications raise questions about informed consent, privacy, access and how benefits and uncertainties are communicated. Environmental applications also require evidence about the affected populations and ecological setting.

A clear response distinguishes scientific findings from value-based choices. Explain what a technology does, what outcomes have actually been measured in the supplied case, and what remains unknown. Do not replace evidence with either enthusiasm about a label or fear of the label.
No personal DNA or family medical information is required for these activities.

extension.question: How can a useful intended effect be evaluated alongside other effects?
sections: A bounded hypothetical case

A hypothetical plant line is engineered to produce a protein that reduces feeding by one insect. In a controlled plot, leaf damage is lower than in an otherwise comparable line. No measurements of other organisms or long-term population changes are supplied.
The result supports reduced damage in the tested conditions. It does not yet answer every question about ecological effects or performance elsewhere.
Identify the next evidence

An evaluation can distinguish the intended trait from unintended changes, compare appropriate controls and consider effects on other organisms. The important measurements depend on the proposed use and exposure.

review.question: Can you connect a DNA sequence with its copying, expression and evidence?
review.goal: Integrate molecular mechanisms, sequence reasoning and interpretation of technology results.
review.prior: Identify the molecule, direction and measured outcome before drawing a conclusion.
sections: Follow information without confusing the molecules

Replication copies DNA through complementary semiconservative synthesis. Transcription uses one template to make RNA, and translation reads mRNA codons to assemble a polypeptide. RNA processing modifies the message without normally deleting introns from the genomic DNA.
A sequence answer should identify the strand and direction, preserve antiparallel pairing and use the correct reading frame. A stop codon is a signal, not an amino acid.
Connect a change with the relevant measurement
A DNA mutation may alter a product, but its effect must be traced through the sequence and biological context. Recombination can create new combinations without a new mutation at every locus.

PCR, gels, sequencing and recombinant-DNA methods provide different kinds of evidence. A complete explanation identifies what each method measures and separates compatibility, expression and function from stronger unsupported claims.
